leapDayModal.howItWorksBody: Regeln werden in einer bestimmten Reihenfolge ausgeführt. Ein Jahr ist ein Schaltjahr, wenn es mit einer Regel übereinstimmt, es sei denn, es entspricht auch einer "Überspringen"-Regel. Zum Beispiel fügt der gregorianische Kalender alle 4 Jahre einen Schalttag hinzu, überspringt das Schaltjahr aber alle 100 Jahre, wenn dieses auch durch 400 teilbar ist.

aliases.howItWorksParagraph1: Aliase sind wie verschiedene Etikette für den gleichen Ordner. Wenn Sie das Konzept erwähnen mit
aliases.howItWorksParagraph1Tail: die Erwähnung verknüpft das Konzept selbst, nicht nur den reinen Text.
aliases.howItWorksParagraph2: Wenn Sie das Konzept oder einen Alias umbenennen, werden verknüpfte Erwähnungen überall automatisch aktualisiert. Verwenden Sie konsequent Erwähnungen, um die Namen in Ihrem gesamten Projekt synchronisiert zu halten.
aliases.howItWorksParagraph3: Wenn Sie ein Alias entfernen, bleiben verknüpfte Erwähnungen erhalten und greifen auf den Konzeptnamen zurück.
aliases.howItWorksParagraph4: Sie können nun auch Konzepte verknüpfen, ohne @ einzugeben. Fangen Sie einfach an einen Konzeptnamen oder einen Alias einzugeben und wenn es eine Übereinstimmung gibt, erscheint ein Vorschlag. Wenn es mehr als einen gibt, verwenden Sie die Pfeiltasten zur Auswahl und drücken dann die Eingabetaste, oder klicken auf den Text, um diesen in eine Verknüpfung umzuwandeln.
aliases.howItWorksParagraph5: Nur weil ein Vorschlag erscheint, ändert sich nichts. Wenn Sie weiterschreiben oder ein Leerzeichen einfügen, bleibt Ihr Text einfach Text. Sie können die Vorschläge auch in den Editor-Ansichtseinstellungen ausschalten, falls diese im Weg umgehen.

nodeSize.title: Scales node size.

centerForce.title: Pulls nodes toward the graph centre.

axisForceX.title: Horizontal pull toward the centre line.

radialForce.title: Pulls nodes toward/around a radius from centre.

orphanOrbitOuterRadius.title: Distance of isolated nodes from the centre when orbit is enabled.

orphanOrbitOuterRadius.decrease: Decrease: isolated nodes orbit closer in.

orphanOrbitStrength.title: How strongly isolated nodes stay on their orbit path.
orphanOrbitStrength.increase: Increase: isolated nodes stick to orbit more firmly.
orphanOrbitStrength.decrease: Decrease: isolated nodes drift more freely.

repelForce.title: How strongly nodes push each other apart.

chargeDistance.title: Maximum distance where node repulsion has effect.
chargeDistance.increase: Increase: repulsion affects nodes from farther away.

linkForce.title: How strongly links pull connected nodes together.
linkForce.decrease: Decrease: connected nodes can drift farther apart.

linkDistance.title: Target length of links between connected nodes.
linkDistance.increase: Increase: connected nodes sit farther apart.
linkDistance.decrease: Decrease: connected nodes sit closer together.

wordUsage.title: Word Usage
wordUsage.vocabularyHint: For fiction, roughly 45-70 often reads natural. Lower can mean repetition or glue-heavy prose; higher can mean dense wording or synonym-chasing.
wordUsage.readabilitySummary: Based on the items below. Demanding text may simply have longer sentences or specialist words.
wordUsage.fleschReferenceHelp: Flesch estimates reading ease from sentence length and syllables. Specialist words can lower the score, so compare it with the reader you are writing for.
wordUsage.readingEaseHelp: A 0-100 Flesch Reading Ease score. Higher usually means quicker to read; lower usually means denser.
wordUsage.gradeLevelHelp: Flesch-Kincaid gives a rough US school grade based on sentence length and syllables. It is about density, not whether the passage is right for your audience.
wordUsage.noReadabilityIssues: No reading effort items to show.

readabilityIssueHelp.adverbs: Shows adverbs and words ending in -ly. They can add nuance; if a line feels slow, check whether the verb already says enough.
readabilityIssueHelp.passiveVoice: Shows likely passive voice, where something has an action done to it. This can be useful when the actor does not matter, and less clear when the actor should be named.
readabilityIssueHelp.complexWording: Shows very long words and a small list of complex words. Technical or science terms may belong here; check whether your reader will know them.
readabilityIssueHelp.hardSentences: Shows sentences of 20-24 words. Long sentences can work well; this helps you find places where readers may need more breath.
readabilityIssueHelp.veryHardSentences: Shows sentences of 25 words or more. These can suit complex action, reflection, or voice; they may just ask more from the reader.
readabilityIssueHelp.wordRepetition: Shows repeated words close together. Repetition can create rhythm, emphasis, or a motif; this helps you spot it.
readabilityIssueHelp.characterRepetition: Shows neighbouring words with matching starts or endings. These echoes can add music, texture, or emphasis; this helps you notice clusters.
readabilityIssueHelp.badStyle: Shows repeated punctuation and informal spellings such as gonna, kinda, or tho. Some belong in voice or dialogue; this makes them easy to check.
readabilityIssueHelp.weakWords: Shows broad or uncertain words such as maybe, somewhat, thing, or seems. They can soften voice or leave room for doubt.
readabilityIssueHelp.strongWords: Shows vivid, precise, or energetic words. Use it to see where the writing has extra charge.

wordUsage.flowHint: Use the chart below to see how sentence length varies across the text.
wordUsage.sentenceRhythmHint: Each bar is a sentence; taller bars mean more words.

openerHelp.dialogue: Starts with quoted dialogue using straight or curly quote marks.
openerHelp.pronoun: Starts with a pronoun, such as she, they, it, or this.
openerHelp.article: Starts with an article: a, an, or the.
openerHelp.conjunction: Starts with a joining word, such as and, but, or because.
openerHelp.preposition: Starts with a relationship word, such as under, near, or with.
openerHelp.adverb: Starts with a known adverb or a word ending in -ly.
openerHelp.properNoun: Starts with a likely specific name. Capitalisation alone is not treated as enough evidence.
openerHelp.other: Does not match one of the opener patterns above.

wordUsage.paragraphDensityHint: Each dot is a paragraph - darker reads denser.
wordUsage.sentenceOpenerHint: What part of speech starts each sentence.
wordUsage.searchHelper: Search or pick a common word to see its usage count.

help.overview: Counts are based on the editor text: words, detected sentences, and average words per sentence.
help.vocabulary: Word variety estimates how many fresh, non-common words appear per 100 words. It describes texture; it is not a quality score.
help.readability: A rough guide to how much effort the text may take to read, based on countable patterns such as sentence length, repetition, passive voice, adverbs, specialist-looking words, vague words, and informal spellings. Demanding text is not necessarily worse; audience, genre, and purpose matter.
help.flow: Each vertical bar is a sentence, coloured by length. Select a length below to highlight every matching sentence in the editor.
help.sentenceLength: Buckets are {{appName}} rhythm markers: 1-8, 9-16, 17-24, and 25+ words. They help spot pacing, not correctness.
help.sentenceRhythm: Each bar represents one sentence. Long passages scroll horizontally so every sentence stays hoverable.
help.structure: Density is based on words per paragraph. Openers use lightweight word-list heuristics for how sentences begin.
help.paragraphDensity: Density is based on words per paragraph: 1-25, 26-60, 61-100, and 101+ words.
help.sentenceOpener: Openers use lightweight word-list heuristics for pronouns, articles, conjunctions, prepositions, adverbs, proper nouns, and other starts.
help.wordUsage: Frequent words come from this project after common stopwords are filtered for the selected spellcheck language.
